title: The Clans of Judah, Jabez's Prayer, and Simeon
summary: The chapter adds more families of Judah, including craftsmen, linen workers, and royal potters, and in the middle of the list pauses for Jabez, whose mother named him for pain and who asked God to bless him and keep him from harm. The second half traces the small tribe of Simeon, lists its towns in the far south, and records how some Simeonite clans took new pasture lands in the days of Hezekiah.
story: The genealogies continue with the southern tribes. Chapter 2 had followed Judah's great clans and chapter 3 the house of David; here the Chronicler gathers remaining branches of Judah and then turns to Simeon, whose territory lay inside Judah's. Two things break the steady flow of names. The first is Jabez, a man of no known family connection who is remembered for a single prayer that God answered. The second is a pair of short reports about Simeonite clans moving out to find pasture and space. Both show what the Chronicler wants his readers to see in their history: God hears those who call on him, and the people's life in the land was never only a matter of names on a list.
historical:
The Judahite families in verses 1 to 23 are tied to towns in the hill country and the lowland (the Shephelah) of Judah, such as Bethlehem, Tekoa, Gedor, Eshtemoa, Soco, Keilah, and Mareshah. Othniel son of Kenaz (verse 13) is the first of the judges (Judges 3:9-11), and Caleb son of Jephunneh (verse 15) is the scout who trusted God in Numbers 13 and 14. The note in verse 22 that these names come from ancient records shows the Chronicler drawing on older sources.

Simeon's towns in verses 28 to 33 closely match Joshua 19:2-8, which says Simeon's inheritance lay within Judah's territory. Over time Simeon seems to have been absorbed into Judah, which may be why the note in verse 27 says its clans did not grow as numerous. Ziklag, listed in verse 30, later passed to David from the Philistine king Achish (1 Samuel 27:6), which may explain the note that these were Simeon's cities until the reign of David. The expansion in verses 39 to 43 is dated to the days of Hezekiah, who reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC. The Meunites were a people of the southern desert who appear again in the reign of Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:7), and the Amalekites were Israel's ancient enemies in the south (Exodus 17; 1 Samuel 15 and 30).
cultural:
Many families in these lists are identified by their work. There were craftsmen at Ge-harashim, whose name means valley of craftsmen (verse 14), linen workers at Beth-ashbea (verse 22), and potters at Netaim and Gederah who lived there in the king's service (verse 23). In ancient Israel trades were often passed down in families and associated with particular towns. Some scholars have connected the royal potters with the many storage jar handles found in Judah stamped with a Hebrew phrase meaning belonging to the king, dated to the late eighth century BC, though the link can't be proved.

Names also carried meaning. Jabez's mother named him because she bore him in pain, and a name like that was not neutral; it could feel like a sentence hanging over a life. His prayer asks God to reverse it. Mered's marriage to Bithiah, called Pharaoh's daughter (verse 18), shows again how outsiders were joined to Judah's families, though whether she was a royal princess or simply an Egyptian woman of standing is unclear. In a pastoral society, pasture was life, and the Simeonites' search for good land for their flocks (verses 39 to 41) reflects the pressures of growing clans with limited territory.
literary: The chapter is a genealogy with short narrative notes set into it. The Jabez passage (verses 9 and 10) stands out sharply: the names on either side of it have no story, and suddenly a man is described as more honorable than his brothers, his mother speaks, he prays, and God answers. The passage turns on a wordplay: the Hebrew name Jabez sounds like the word for pain with two consonants swapped, and his prayer asks to be free from that very pain. The Simeon section follows a pattern the Chronicler uses for several tribes: descendants, towns, a list of leaders, and a short account of a military success or settlement. The repeated phrase to this day (verses 41 and 43) links the old events with the situation the first readers knew.

outline.t: Further families of Judah, including craftsmen and potters
The descendants and towns of Simeon
Simeonite leaders and their expansion to new pasture lands

doctrines.note: Jabez's prayer is the Chronicler's first example of a pattern the book repeats: someone calls on God in need, and God answers. The prayer is simple and honest, asking for blessing, room, God's presence, and protection from harm.

Ordinary families of potters, craftsmen, and shepherds are recorded by name. The chapter treats their work and their search for pasture as part of Israel's life under God, not as something beneath his notice.

The Simeonites' attack on the remnant of the Amalekites recalls the long conflict between Israel and Amalek. It is reported briefly, and the Chronicler neither dwells on it nor explains it, leaving the reader with the harder question of how such warfare fits God's purposes.

words.note: Jabez. The name sounds like a scrambled form of the Hebrew word for pain, and verse 9 makes the connection explicit. Nothing else is known of him, not even his father's name. He is remembered only because he prayed.

Otsev, pain or sorrow, the reason for Jabez's name. Related words appear in Genesis 3:16-17, where pain in childbirth and painful toil are part of the curse after the fall. Jabez's prayer asks God to free him from the pain his birth had spoken over him.

Barak, to bless. When God blesses in the Old Testament, he gives life, fruitfulness, and well-being. Jabez asks for blessing in concrete terms, land and safety, the ordinary goods of life in ancient Israel.

Yachas, to be enrolled in a genealogy (verse 33). It is a characteristic word of Chronicles and of Ezra-Nehemiah, reflecting the post-exilic concern with registered family lines. To be enrolled was to have a recognized place in the people of God.

christ: The Jabez passage shows a man asking to be delivered from the pain written into his life from birth, and God granting it. The New Testament speaks of a greater reversal: Jesus bore our griefs and sorrows (as Isaiah 53:4 had said of the servant of the LORD) so that the curse of pain and toil introduced in Genesis 3 would not have the final word. Revelation 21:4 looks toward a day when there will be no more pain. That connection is thematic rather than predictive; Jabez is not a figure of Christ. What the passage does anticipate is the confidence the New Testament gives believers to bring their needs to God, who hears.

hard.q: Is the prayer of Jabez a formula for success and prosperity?
hard.a:
In 2000 Bruce Wilkinson's book The Prayer of Jabez became a bestseller, encouraging Christians to pray these words daily and expect God to expand their influence and blessing. Many readers found the book an encouragement to pray boldly. Many others, including a large number of pastors and scholars, worried that it turned a brief narrative into a formula and could slide toward prosperity teaching, the idea that God rewards faith with material gain.

The text itself is modest. It reports that one man, remembered as honorable, prayed for blessing, land, God's hand, and freedom from harm, and that God answered. The Chronicler presents this as an example of a pattern he values: those who call on the God of Israel are heard. Nothing in the passage suggests that repeating Jabez's words guarantees a result, and elsewhere Scripture shows faithful people who prayed and suffered. The best reading lets Jabez teach honest, confident prayer to a God who cares about ordinary needs, while leaving the answer in God's hands.

questions: Jabez's mother named him for her pain. Are there words spoken over your life that you have needed God to reverse?
The chapter honors potters, linen workers, and shepherds by name. How does God's attention to ordinary work change the way you think about your own?
What is the difference between praying boldly for God's blessing and treating prayer as a technique to get what we want?
